passage: By October Damini had twelve small students on the veranda in three batches, from four in the afternoon till nine at night. The first fee money had made her giddy, and every new child felt like another win. The steel tin behind the rice sack grew heavy. But her own homework was done on the bus, half-copied, and she slept five hours. In the monthly test her maths marks fell from sixty-eight to forty-one. “Your notebook's empty,” her friend Ira said at lunch. Damini snapped that she was earning. That night she sat with the marked test in one hand and the tin in the other, counting both. The rupees suddenly looked small beside everything they had cost.

qa.q: How many students did Damini have by October?
What was Damini feeling when Ira said the notebook was empty?
qa.a: Defensive and stung: she snapped that she was earning, though the falling marks were already worrying her.

qa.q: What could Damini do instead, and why might it work?
qa.a: She could keep only a few students on fixed evenings and protect sleep and homework time, because steady marks and rest matter more than extra money.

qa.q: How might Ira see Damini's plan?
qa.a: Ira sees a friend who is tired, short-tempered and behind on homework, and worries that the tutoring is costing more than it earns.

grounding: Excited by early earnings, a student takes on many tutees, and homework, sleep and marks suffer.
